sbh4.3:1.1: Paragraph 1 maps each meditative attainment to its corresponding rebirth: each of the four *dhyāna*s and the four *ārūpya* attainments has a three-tier (mild/middling/strong) cultivation that yields rebirth in a specific tier of the corresponding deva-realm. This is the *bhāvanā-phala* mapping that completes the *laukika-mārga* analysis of [sbh4.1](sbh4.1.html)–[sbh4.2](sbh4.2.html). The five Pure Abode gods (Avṛha through Akaniṣṭha) are the realms of *anāgāmin* rebirth — the supramundane fourth-dhyāna mixing with-flux and fluxless cultivation produces a fivefold result (1.6–1.8). The standard Sarvāstivāda *Abhidharmakośa* III scheme is identical in structure though with different deva-list orderings.
sbh4.3:3.1: The *sapta-manaskāra* (seven attentions) — *lakṣaṇa-pratisaṃvedī* (characteristic-knowing), *ādhimokṣika* (resolve-born), *prāvivekya* (seclusion), *rati-saṃgrāhaka* (delight-collecting), *mīmāṃsā* (investigation), *prayoga-niṣṭhā* (practice-culmination), *prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala* (fruit-of-practice-culmination) — were treated in detail under the *laukika-mārga* at [sbh4.1](sbh4.1.html). Here they are reused for the *lokottara-mārga*: the *same seven* applied to the *different object* (four noble truths instead of grossness/calmness). This is the chapter's central architectural argument: the seven-attention progression is the *general* form of meditative progression, applicable equally to laukika and lokottara. Compare [sbh3.1:15.2](sbh3.1.html#sbh3.1:15.2) for the same reusability claim about the four *manaskāra* across śamatha and vipaśyanā.
sbh4.3:3.5: The *ṣoḍaśa-ākāra ārya-satya* — sixteen aspects of the four noble truths — is the canonical Sarvāstivāda-Yogācāra analytic framework. Four truths × four aspects = sixteen aspects. Of suffering: *anitya, duḥkha, śūnya, anātma* (impermanence, suffering, emptiness, not-self). Of arising: *hetu, samudaya, prabhava, pratyaya* (cause, arising, origination, condition). Of cessation: *nirodha, śānta, praṇīta, niḥsaraṇa* (cessation, calm, sublime, escape). Of path: *mārga, nyāya, pratipatti, nairyāṇika* (path, method, practice, deliverance). The original at 3.5 dropped *śūnyatā*; restored in brackets. The same sixteen are taken as the object of the *darśana-mārga* sixteen-moment penetration in *Abhidharmakośa* VI.27.
sbh4.3:4.3: The ten aspects of suffering at 4.3–4.5 unfold the four aspects of *duḥkha-satya* in finer grain. Mapping (made explicit at 23.1–5): *anityatā* is comprised by five aspects — *vipariṇāma* (transformation), *vināśa* (destruction), *viyoga* (separation), *sannihita* (at-hand), *dharmatā* (nature-of-things). *duḥkhatā* is comprised by three aspects — *saṃyojana-bandhana* (fetter-and-bondage), *aniṣṭa* (unwished-for), *anāśvāsika* (insecurity). *śūnyatā* is comprised by one aspect — *anupalabdhi* (non-apprehension). *anātmatā* is comprised by one aspect — *asvatantra* (non-autonomy). The 5+3+1+1 partition is canonical and gives a doctrinal reason for the unequal weighting: impermanence is multi-modal (five distinct ways things change), suffering is tri-modal (three distinct ways things hurt), and emptiness/no-self are each grounded in a single decisive epistemological insight.
sbh4.3:4.5: Note: the original at 4.5 named the ninth aspect *anugraha* (non-assistance/non-helpfulness), but the actual analysis at 22.34 clearly identifies it as *anupalabdhi* (non-apprehension) — the aspect by which the practitioner enters *śūnyatā*. Corrected to non-apprehension to match the analysis-passage. *anupalabdhi* is the standard Yogācāra epistemological term for what the meditator *fails to find* when looking for a self among the aggregates: 'mere aggregate, no self.'
sbh4.3:6.7: Scribal duplication: 6.7–6.10 partially repeat 6.1–6.6 before the proper definition of outward-substance resumes at 6.11. The duplication appears mid-sentence (6.7 starts with the correct definition of inward-substance, then breaks off into a re-quotation of the introductory material). Preserved as-is, but flagged. The text resumes cleanly at 6.11 with the sixteenfold outward-substance enumeration.
sbh4.3:8.7: Scribal slip: 8.7 mistakenly says water 'burns' (read up from 8.6 about fire-burning) — corrected to 'floods' at 8.8 immediately. Both versions preserved.
sbh4.3:21.1: The anti-Īśvara refutation at 21.1–21.10 is a compact reductio: if Īśvara is a creation-cause, either (a) creation is unmediated, in which case Īśvara and creation must be simultaneous (refuted: they are not); or (b) creation is mediated by Īśvara's resolve, in which case the resolve is either caused or uncaused (caused leads to regress; uncaused implies creation by Īśvara is itself causally indeterminate and not 'by Īśvara' in any robust sense). This is shared technical material with Vasubandhu's *Abhidharmakośa* II's anti-Īśvara refutation, with Dignāga's logical school, and (later) with Dharmakīrti's *Pramāṇavārttika* II. The Yogācāra position throughout is that this-world variation is *karma*-conditioned, not Īśvara-conditioned.
sbh4.3:22.32: The 'mere aggregate, no self' analysis at 22.26–34 is the canonical *nairātmya* argument: faculties alone are perceived, sense-objects alone, mere experience born from that, mere mind, mere name, mere seeing, mere designation — nothing beyond, nothing further. Through *anupalabdhi* (non-apprehension) the practitioner enters *śūnyatā*. Through *asvatantra* (non-autonomy: dependent arising entails non-autonomy entails not-self) the practitioner enters *anātmatā*. The two together complete the truth-of-suffering analysis. Note the deliberate epistemological framing: it is not that there *is* no self but that no self *is found* — Yogācāra characteristic epistemic restraint.
sbh4.3:26.17: The *nirvedha-bhāgīya* progression at 26.17–19 maps onto the *ākāra* attainment via patience-grades: mild patience → *ūṣma-gata* (warmth); middling patience → *mūrdhan* (summits); strong patience → middling-conforming patience (*madhya-satya-anulomikī kṣānti*) — and (continuing into 27) the *laukikāgra-dharma* arises immediately before the *darśana-mārga* proper at 27.14. The fire-stick simile at [sbh2.0:82.12](sbh2.0.html#sbh2.0:82.12) is the canonical figure for this same progression: warmth → smoke → flameless fire → flame.
sbh4.3:27.4: The remarkable description at 27.3–11 of the mind appearing 'as if ceased,' 'as if without object,' 'as if gone away' — but not actually ceased, not actually without object, not actually gone away — is the canonical phenomenology of the *laukikāgra-dharma* (supreme worldly dharmas) moment. The mind reaches a state that *resembles* nirvāṇa (no object grasped, no defilement active) without yet *being* nirvāṇa. The warning at 27.10 that 'for some dull, perplexed ones this state becomes overweening' acknowledges that this resemblance can mislead a practitioner into thinking they have attained more than they have — only the immediately-following moment (27.14: *laukikāgra-dharma*) and then the *darśana-mārga* (27.18+) constitute the actual entry into the noble lineage.
sbh4.3:27.14: *laukikāgra-dharma* (supreme worldly dharmas) — the last moment of mundane consciousness before the *darśana-mārga* begins. As 27.17 says, 'this is the limit, the end of mundane formations.' Canonically the very last of the four *nirvedha-bhāgīya* (warmth, summits, patience, supreme-worldly-dharma), positioned at the gate between *prayoga-mārga* and *darśana-mārga*. From here the supramundane mind alone arises (27.15). See also [sbh2.0:67.19](sbh2.0.html#sbh2.0:67.19) for the canonical four-fold *nirvedha-bhāgīya* schema.
sbh4.3:28.5: *anāgāmin* (non-returner) — the third of the four fruits of asceticism (cf. [sbh2.0:88.4](sbh2.0.html#sbh2.0:88.4) for the canonical defilement-mapping: abandonment of the five lower fetters yields the non-returner). The chapter at 28.3–14 gives the alternate path-orderings depending on the practitioner's prior degree of dispassion: if previously without-lust toward sense-pleasures at supramundane-darśana, immediately to anāgāmin; if more strongly without-lust, to *sakṛdāgāmin*; if still with-lust, to *srotāpanna*. This is an unusual non-sequential treatment — most Sarvāstivāda accounts have stream-entry first and then later progression — but is consistent with the *Śrāvakabhūmi*'s persistent emphasis that path-stage depends on faculty-condition at the moment of *darśana*, not on a forced sequential schema.
sbh4.3:28.38: The four *avetya-prasāda* (serenities of clear knowing) — confidence in Buddha, dharma, saṅgha, and the noble training (*ārya-śīla*) — are canonical and treated at [sbh2.0:81.27](sbh2.0.html#sbh2.0:81.27) as the predominant-effect of the *śraddhā-indriya*. Their reappearance here at 28.38 as a sign of stream-entry confirms the Sarvāstivāda standard: the four *avetya-prasāda* are precisely what mark out the stream-enterer (no more doubt about the three jewels and the training) as opposed to the pre-noble practitioner.
sbh4.3:29.1: The elevenfold *bhāvanā-prabheda* (cultivation-typing) at 29.1–7 is the chapter's culminating typology: śamatha-cultivation, vipaśyanā-cultivation, mundane-path-cultivation, supramundane-path-cultivation, three by intensity (mild, middling, strong), and the four-fold *mārga* division — *prayoga-mārga* (preparation), *ānantarya-mārga* (immediacy), *vimukti-mārga* (liberation), *viśeṣa-mārga* (distinction). The same four-fold *mārga* analysis appears in Sarvāstivāda *Abhidharmakośa* VI.65–67 as the structure within each of the *darśana-* and *bhāvanā-mārga*. Each fruit (stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship) is attained via this four-fold internal sequence — preparation establishes the conditions, *ānantarya-mārga* is the actual moment of defilement-abandonment, *vimukti-mārga* is the moment of post-abandonment freedom, *viśeṣa-mārga* is the consolidation thereof.
